headline: Guatemala: Mayan Roots to Modern Struggles
text: This documentary frames Guatemala through the lens of its ancient Mayan roots, tracing the civilization from its origins around 2,000 BC through its architectural and intellectual peak in the classic period, when city-states like Tikal and El Mirador built pyramids and developed writing, math, and astronomy. It shows how that world declined in the south but persisted in the north until the Spanish arrived.

headline: Guatemala: Mayan Roots to Modern Struggles
text: The video then moves through Guatemala's colonial and modern political history: Spanish conquest in the early 1500s, a bumpy road to full independence by 1839, decades of dictatorship tied to the United Fruit Company, a brief democratic window from 1945-1954 ended by a US-backed coup, and a brutal 36-year civil war that specifically targeted indigenous Mayans before ending in 1996.

headline: Guatemala: Mayan Roots to Modern Struggles
text: Culturally, the film paints Guatemala as majority indigenous, with Mayans making up 40-60% of the population and speaking over 20 distinct languages, while religion blends Catholic and Protestant practice with indigenous spiritual traditions tied to nature and the Mayan calendar.

text: Economically, Guatemala is described as agriculture-driven, a top global exporter of coffee and bananas, with tourism and manufacturing playing supporting roles, but the country still struggles with deep inequality, corruption, and heavy reliance on the US as its top trade partner.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
text: A geneticist-historian walks through genetics' rare self-imposed research pauses to argue the public, not just scientists, must decide how far gene editing goes.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
text: Matthew Cobb, a zoologist and science historian at the University of Manchester, joins This Week in Science to discuss his book As Gods: A Moral History of the Genetic Age. His interest in blending science and history began with an unusually mixed UK education and deepened while researching insect olfaction in France, where he stumbled on 17th-century texts that hooked him on the field's past. The book's throughline is a striking fact: genetics is the only scientific field where researchers have voluntarily paused their own work, four separate times, out of fear of the consequences.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
text: Cobb walks through the landmark 1972 and 1975 Asilomar meetings, where roughly 200 scientists debated how to safely handle recombinant DNA but never asked whether they should be doing it at all -- and crucially, did so without public input. That self-regulation model, he argues, set a pattern of condescension toward the public that persists today. The controversy faded by 1980 once experiments proved safe and money started flowing, the same year Genentech and Apple both went public.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
text: The conversation turns dark with the 2018 He Jiankui scandal, where a Chinese scientist edited human embryos that became three girls carrying unprecedented, heritable mutations, despite there being no real medical need since existing IVF techniques already let most affected couples have healthy biological children. Cobb calls it a solution in search of a question, criticizing figures like Elon Musk for fantasizing about genetically modifying humans for life on Mars, and notes that even CRISPR's own inventors split on whether a moratorium was warranted.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
text: Gene drives get a nuanced treatment: Cobb refuses to be simply anti-technology, stressing that 600,000 malaria deaths a year, mostly children, are the real stakes, and that researchers pursuing gene drives are thoughtful, not reckless -- one even hid his breakthrough from his supervisor out of fear. But he flags unknown ecological risks, the existence of simpler alternatives like a newly approved malaria vaccine, and a glaring consent problem: villages in places like Burkina Faso have no word for 'gene' yet are expected to approve trials that, given how mosquitoes travel, will affect regions far beyond their borders.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
text: Cobb closes by arguing that genetic technology urgently needs the kind of international oversight aviation and nuclear power already have, but doubts governments currently have the appetite for it. His core message is that history shows genetics' worst fears often didn't come true, but the public was never actually invited to help decide -- and that omission, not the science itself, is the deeper problem.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
text: Genetics uniquely polices itself — Cobb argues no other scientific field, not even nuclear physics during the Manhattan Project, has ever voluntarily paused its own research out of safety fears -- genetics has done it four times.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
text: Asilomar asked 'how,' never 'should we' — The famous 1972/75 meetings on recombinant DNA safety were entirely scientist-run and focused only on biosecurity, never on whether the research should happen or including public voices.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
text: The embryo-editing scandal had no real need — Cobb argues He Jiankui's 2018 experiment served almost no one, since couples with genetic disease can already have healthy biological children via IVF and embryo selection -- true embryo editing might help only a few hundred couples worldwide.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
text: Heritable edits are irreversible — Unlike therapy on an adult's own cells, editing embryos changes genes that get passed to all future descendants -- a mutation introduced now is, in Cobb's words, forever.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
text: CRISPR's inventors disagreed on a pause — Emmanuelle Charpentier signed a call for a moratorium on embryo editing; Jennifer Doudna did not, believing it was already too late to stop -- a split Cobb thinks is wrong.

headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
